reflection_text.5:
The question is about Dvořák B.12 Symphony No.2. The confusion is Op.4 original vs Op.22 performing transposition.

Original Op.4 B.12 = 1865 D-major symphony. Later revised, transposed down a major third to B♭ major and published as Op.22, the version normally played today and now habitually cited as “Sym. No.2 Op.4”.

Transposition mapping is B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. Hence
Op.22 performing close: Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4 in score order, i.e. B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending, pitch set B♭–D–F. In descending reading last attack = tonic B♭, lowest of the three successive attacks, ~B♭4 just above middle C.
Op.4 original close: same music in D major, engraved F♯–A–D up, read down A–F♯–D. Pitch set F♯–A–D, three distinct pitch classes of D-major tonic. In descending reading last attack = tonic D and that D is the lowest of the three successive attacks, the note on which the orchestra is held. In the upward written order F♯ is the lowest written note.

Current round 2 split persists.

Colleagues 1,6,7 maintain the performing-edition identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major work, coda F5–D5–B♭4, three pitches B♭–D–F, lowest/last = tonic B♭. Colleague 1 now explicitly notes the F5–D5–B♭4 F–D–B♭ closure is the B♭ equivalent of the A–F♯–D tonic arpeggio quoted for the D-major reading. Colleague 6 notes the same B♭ reading is the performing transposition of the autograph and that transposed back B♭→D etc gives A–F♯–D with tonic D as last/lowest in original key. Colleague 7 insists the D-major/A–F♯–D readings are a mistaken identification and that in catalogue and normal performing material Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12 is B♭ major, lowest B♭.

Colleagues 3,4,5,8 defend the Op.4 original key.
Colleague 3: B.12 is the 1865/70 D-major symphony; Op.22 is the later revision transposed to B♭. For B.12 as written Op.4 the 4th mvt closes tutti in D major on D-major tonic triad A–F♯–D, last/lowest = tonic D. The familiar F5–D5–B♭4 is the Op.22 transposition.
Colleague 4: Symphony No.2 B.12 Op.4 is the 1865 D-major symphony. In autograph/Op.4 original IV closes tutti in D, first-violin coda engraved F♯–A–D read as descent A–F♯–D. Three pitch classes F♯,A,D, last attack tonic D, lowest of A–F♯–D. B♭–D–F / F5–D5–B♭4 is the Op.22 transposition.
Colleague 5: Op.4 B.12 signed by Dvořák is 1865 D-major; later revised transposed down a major third and published as Op.22 in B♭, the version now in everyday use. In genuine Op.4 original IV closes tutti in D major, part termination engraved F♯–A–D written up read down A–F♯–D. Three pitches A,F♯,D, last attack tonic D and lowest. The familiar F5–D5–B♭4/ B♭–D–F descent and “lowest = B♭” is the transposed Op.22/B♭ performing version; B♭ is lowest only in that later transposition.
Colleague 8: Op. number is decisive. B.12 Symphony No.2 Op.4 1870/72 is the D major symphony of 1865. Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major, first-violin coda D major tonic triad broken, printed up as F♯–A–D read as descent A–F♯–D. Last attack tonic D, lowest of three successive attacks. Upward written order F♯ is lowest written attack. B♭–D–F / F5–D5–B♭4 is the 1888 revision/performance transposition published as Op.22.

Colleague 2 is now hedging: describes the edition normally quoted as Sym. No.2 in B♭ major Op.4 B.12 with close F5–D5–B♭4, last attack tonic B♭ lowest. Adds musicological note that autograph Op.4 was originally in D major and later transposed down a major third to B♭ for Op.22; in original D-major autograph same figure is A–F♯–D, original-key pitch-class reading is tonic D as lowest.

Earlier belief remains: for the genuine Op.4 original the pitch name is unequivocally D, the tonic of D major, for the Op.22/B♭ performing version the lowest note is the tonic B♭. The persistent error driving the B♭ consensus is conflating Op.4 with its Op.22 transposition.

Unresolved nuance: exact octave designation in specific edition – D5 in violin staff vs scientific pitch naming, and whether “F♯ is lowest in upward engraving” is an artefact of reading direction. Pitch class is settled: D in original, B♭ in transposed performing edition.

The question as phrased “Symphony no. 2, Op.4” points historically to the D-major original, lowest/last first-violin note D. If the common modern performing identification is intended, the answer quoted is B♭.

In the genuine Op.4 autograph the IV. Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major on the D-major tonic triad. In the first-violin part the coda is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved

    F♯ – A – D

and read in the part as the descent

    A – F♯ – D

which is then held with the fermata on the final D-major sonority. The three distinct pitch classes that the 1st desk actually attacks at the very close are therefore the members of the D-major triad

    F♯, A, D

and in the normal descending A > F♯ > D reading the last attack of the movement in the firsts, the note on which the whole orchestra is held on the fermata, is the tonic D itself, the lowest of the three successive first-violin attacks with which the symphony is left in its original Op.4 key. In the upward written order F♯–A–D the lowest written attack is F♯.

That is the Op.4 reading. 

B♭ → D, D → F♯, F → A

F5 – D5 – B♭4 in score order, i.e. B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending, is the transposed equivalent of the original A–F♯–D / F♯–A–D termination. In the Op.22 / B♭-major performing transposition that is normally quoted today as “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12” the three first-violin pitches of the close are B♭ – D – F and the bottom and final first-violin note of the gesture in the performing edition is the tonic B♭, conventionally written B♭4 in the modern edition, the B♭-major equivalent of the original tonic D.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Op.4 / B.12 identity split is now explicit in the public record.

Performing/revised B♭-major reading, public majority:
* Colleagues 1,2,7 state the edition catalogued and performed today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the revised/Op.22 B♭-major version. IV closes tutti in B♭ major. First-violin coda is tonic arpeggio written in score order Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, same pitch-class set as ascending B♭4 – D5 – F5. Three attacks are B♭, D, F. Last attack held with fermata is tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 ≈466 Hz, the lowest of the three successive attacks in the descending reading. Colleagues 1 and 2 now add musicological notes that this is the transposition of the autograph.

Original-autograph D-major reading:
* Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 hold B.12 as signed 1865/70 is the D-major symphony; Op.22 is the 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major. In the genuine Op.4 autograph IV Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major. First-violin coda is D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order as descent A – F♯ – D. Three pitch classes attacked are F♯, A, D. In descending reading the last and lowest successive attack is tonic D, the note held with final fermata; in upward written order F♯–A–D the lowest written attack is F♯ ≈F♯4. The persistent claim is that the Op.4 reading is D as final/lowest successive attack, F♯ as lowest written attack.

Transposition mapping consistently given: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. Hence performing F5–D5–B♭4 = original A–F♯–D. B♭ is lowest only in the transposed performing version; D is lowest in original key.

Unresolved intent: whether the question intends the standard published/performing B♭-major version, in which the lowest first-violin pitch of the closing three-note figure is B♭, or the original-autograph D-major Op.4 reading, in which the three pitch classes are F♯, A, D and the last/lowest successive attack is tonic D with F♯ the lowest written attack in the upward engraving. Octave placement varies by edition but pitch-class content is either B♭–D–F in the B♭ performing edition or F♯–A–D in the D-major original. The persistent B♭ answers remain the majority public position, while the D-major/original-transposition argument is now more explicitly articulated and acknowledged even by B♭-major colleagues.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about B.12 Symphony No.2. Historically Op.4 B.12 is the 1865/70 D-major autograph. In 1888 Dvořák revised the work, transposing it down a major third to B♭ major and publishing the revision as Op.22. That B♭ version is what is in everyday use today and is habitually cited in libraries and performance material as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Transposition is B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. Hence the same closing figure is

* Op.4 original D major: first-violin coda engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order as descent A–F♯–D. Pitch-class set F♯, A, D. Last attack = tonic D, which is also the lowest of the three successive attacks in the descending reading. Written-up order lowest written pitch is F♯.

* Op.22 / performing B♭ major: first-violin coda Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4 in score order, i.e. B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending. Pitch-class set B♭, D, F. Last attack = tonic B♭, which is also the bottom of the descending F–D–B♭ arpeggio.

Colleagues 1,2,7 now explicitly maintain the performing-edition identification: the edition catalogued as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12 today is B♭ major, last three first-violin attacks F5–D5–B♭4, lowest/last = tonic B♭, ~B♭4. Colleague 1 and 2 now note the musicological caveat that this F–D–B♭ close is the B♭ transposition of the original A–F♯–D figure.

Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 defend the catalogue/Op. number reading: B.12 Op.4 is the D-major original, closes on D-major tonic triad A–F♯–D with tonic D as last/lowest first-violin note. They identify F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F as the Op.22 transposition.

Colleague 2 is hedging, giving the B♭ performing answer first and then the D-major autograph note.

Errors / corrections noted: earlier odd readings e.g. G–A–B♭ turn and F5–B♭5–D6 etc have been superseded in round 3 by the consistent F5–D5–B♭4 / A–F♯–D description.

Unresolved nuance remains octave nomenclature in specific editions and whether “lowest” is read as lowest written attack vs lowest sounding successive attack in descending reading. Pitch-class is settled: D in the genuine Op.4 original, B♭ in the Op.22/B♭ performing transposition that is commonly mislabelled Op.4.

Current understanding therefore is dual: historically correct Op.4 B.12 ends on D; the work most people mean when they say “Symphony No.2 Op.4” today ends on B♭. The persistent source of disagreement is conflation of Op.4 with its Op.22 transposition.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The work is B.12, signed Symphony No.2 Op.4 in 1865/70. Musicologically the autograph Op.4 is in D major; the 1888 revision was transposed down a major third to B♭ major and published as Op.22. The edition in everyday use and universally labelled today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major performing/revised Breitkopf & Härtel version.

In that performing edition IV. Allegro vivace/Allegro con brio closes tutti in B♭ major. The first-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic triad broken as a closing arpeggio. In score order it is written Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, the same pitch-class set as the ascending reading B♭4 – D5 – F5. The three distinct attacks made at the very close are the three members of the tonic triad B♭, D, F. In the descending reading the last attack held with the fermata is also the bottom of the arpeggio: the tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 in modern printing, ~B♭3/4 in older engraving, ≈466 Hz, the lowest of the three first-violin pitches F–D–B♭.

The strict catalogue position, now strongly articulated by colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 in round 3, is that Op.4 B.12 denotes the 1865/70 D-major autograph, not the later transposition. In the original key the same figure is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and read in the part as the descent A – F♯ – D. The three distinct pitch classes attacked are A, F♯, D. In the normal descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack and the bottom of the arpeggio is the tonic D, conventionally about D5 in the first-violin staff, the transposed equivalent of the performing B♭.

Colleagues 1,2,7 maintain the performed identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 as catalogued and performed today = B♭ major, lowest first-violin pitch = tonic B♭, with the musicological note that this is B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A of the original D-major A–F♯–D close.

Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 insist the Op.4 label strictly denotes the D-major autograph, lowest = tonic D, and that F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F is the Op.22/B♭-major transposition habitually cited under the Op.4 number.

Unresolved technical points persist: exact octave nomenclature B♭4 vs B♭3/4, and whether “three notes” is meant as the three successive attacks F–D–B♭ before the sustained final chord or the sustained triad itself. Pitch-class answer is stable under the performing edition = tonic B♭; under the strict original Op.4 identification = tonic D, with B♭ being the transposed equivalent.

* Colleague 2 has moved to the B♭-major performing reading for the edition normally quoted as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12, with an explicit musicological note that the autograph Op.4 was originally D major and later transposed to B♭ for Op.22. In the edition most players use and which is universally identified today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12, the first-violin three-note close is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest note is the tonic B♭, written as B♭4 in the modern edition, the last attack of the descent.

reflection_text.6:

reflection_text.5:
The question is about B.12 Symphony No.2. Historically Op.4 B.12 is the 1865/70 D-major autograph. In 1888 Dvořák revised the work, transposing it down a major third to B♭ major and publishing the revision as Op.22. That B♭ version is what is in everyday use today and is habitually cited in libraries and performance material as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Transposition is B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. Hence the same closing figure is

* Op.4 original D major: first-violin coda engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order as descent A–F♯–D. Pitch-class set F♯, A, D. Last attack = tonic D, which is also the lowest of the three successive attacks in the descending reading. Written-up order lowest written pitch is F♯.

* Op.22 / performing B♭ major: first-violin coda Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4 in score order, i.e. B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending. Pitch-class set B♭, D, F. Last attack = tonic B♭, which is also the bottom of the descending F–D–B♭ arpeggio.

Colleagues 1,2,7 now explicitly maintain the performing-edition identification: the edition catalogued as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12 today is B♭ major, last three first-violin attacks F5–D5–B♭4, lowest/last = tonic B♭, ~B♭4. Colleague 1 and 2 now note the musicological caveat that this F–D–B♭ close is the B♭ transposition of the original A–F♯–D figure.

Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 defend the catalogue/Op. number reading: B.12 Op.4 is the D-major original, closes on D-major tonic triad A–F♯–D with tonic D as last/lowest first-violin note. They identify F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F as the Op.22 transposition.

Colleague 2 is hedging, giving the B♭ performing answer first and then the D-major autograph note.

Errors / corrections noted: earlier odd readings e.g. G–A–B♭ turn and F5–B♭5–D6 etc have been superseded in round 3 by the consistent F5–D5–B♭4 / A–F♯–D description.

Unresolved nuance remains octave nomenclature in specific editions and whether “lowest” is read as lowest written attack vs lowest sounding successive attack in descending reading. Pitch-class is settled: D in the genuine Op.4 original, B♭ in the Op.22/B♭ performing transposition that is commonly mislabelled Op.4.

Current understanding therefore is dual: historically correct Op.4 B.12 ends on D; the work most people mean when they say “Symphony No.2 Op.4” today ends on B♭. The persistent source of disagreement is conflation of Op.4 with its Op.22 transposition.
reflection_text.7:
The work is B.12, signed Symphony No.2 Op.4 in 1865/70. Musicologically the autograph Op.4 is in D major; the 1888 revision was transposed down a major third to B♭ major and published as Op.22. The edition in everyday use and universally labelled today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major performing/revised Breitkopf & Härtel version.

In that performing edition IV. Allegro vivace/Allegro con brio closes tutti in B♭ major. The first-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic triad broken as a closing arpeggio. In score order it is written Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, the same pitch-class set as the ascending reading B♭4 – D5 – F5. The three distinct attacks made at the very close are the three members of the tonic triad B♭, D, F. In the descending reading the last attack held with the fermata is also the bottom of the arpeggio: the tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 in modern printing, ~B♭3/4 in older engraving, ≈466 Hz, the lowest of the three first-violin pitches F–D–B♭.

The strict catalogue position, now strongly articulated by colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 in round 3, is that Op.4 B.12 denotes the 1865/70 D-major autograph, not the later transposition. In the original key the same figure is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and read in the part as the descent A – F♯ – D. The three distinct pitch classes attacked are A, F♯, D. In the normal descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack and the bottom of the arpeggio is the tonic D, conventionally about D5 in the first-violin staff, the transposed equivalent of the performing B♭.

Colleagues 1,2,7 maintain the performed identification: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 as catalogued and performed today = B♭ major, lowest first-violin pitch = tonic B♭, with the musicological note that this is B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A of the original D-major A–F♯–D close.

The Op.4 catalogue number is B.12 1865/70.

B.12 as signed by Dvořák is the D-major symphony. Op.22 is the 1888 revision of the same music transposed down a major third to B♭ major and is the version that is in everyday use and that is habitually cited in modern libraries and performance material as “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12”.

In the genuine Op.4 / B.12 autograph

IV. Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major on the D-major tonic triad. In the engraving it is written up

Vln I  F♯ – A – D

and read in the part as the descent

Vln I  A – F♯ – D

on the final D-major fermata. The three distinct pitch classes actually attacked by the 1st desk at the very close are therefore A, F♯ and D.

In the normal descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack of the gesture is the tonic itself and it is the bottom of the arpeggio, the note on which the whole orchestra is held with the final D-major fermata. Vln I  F5 – D5 – B♭4  ≡  B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending

i.e. the B♭-major tonic triad B♭ – D – F. The last and bottom attack in that performing edition is the tonic B♭, conventionally written B♭4 in the modern edition, the transposed equivalent of the original Op.4 tonic D.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The work is B.12, signed Symphony No.2 Op.4 in 1865/70. Autograph/genuine Op.4 is D major; the 1888 revision/transposition down a major third to B♭ major was published as Op.22 and is the version in everyday use and habitually cited today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Coda of IV Allegro vivace/Allegro molto:
* Original Op.4 D-major autograph: first-violin coda is the D-major tonic broken chord, engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order A–F♯–D. Three distinct pitch classes A, F♯, D. In descending reading the last attack/lowest of the three successive notes is tonic D. This is maintained by Colleagues 3,4,5,7.
* Performing/revised B♭-major edition, the edition universally quoted today as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12: first-violin Vln I in score order F5–D5–B♭4, i.e. pitch-class set B♭4–D5–F5 ascending. Three distinct attacks are B♭–D–F. Last attack is tonic B♭, also bottom of descending arpeggio. This is stated as primary by Colleagues 1,2,6,8 and acknowledged as the transposed equivalent by all.

Transposition map is now explicitly acknowledged by all: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A; so B♭-major F–D–B♭ = D-major A–F♯–D.

Round 0 errors corrected in prior rounds: Colleague 4’s F5–B♭5–D6 / “lowest degree D” retracted to F5–D5–B♭4 / tonic B♭ lowest; Colleague 7’s G–A–B♭ turn retracted.

Round 4 consensus: Colleagues 1,2,6,8 give the performing edition answer as primary: lowest first-violin note is tonic B♭, written B♭4 ~ B♭3 in older engraving, last of F5–D5–B♭4 descending ≡ B♭4–D5–F5 ascending. Colleagues 3,4,5,7 give the catalogue-original answer as primary: lowest first-violin note in the genuine Op.4 B.12 autograph is tonic D, last of A–F♯–D descending ≡ F♯–A–D engraved up, and note that B♭ is the transposed equivalent in Op.22.

Unresolved is intent of the question: original Op.4 D-major autograph → pitch-class answer D, lowest first-violin note tonic D; or standard modern performing edition commonly called Symphony No.2 Op.4 → pitch-class answer B♭, lowest first-violin note tonic B♭.

My current best belief remains the conventional modern performing reading quoted in the deliberation: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 as performed today is in B♭ major, first-violin final three pitches F5–D5–B♭4 descending ≡ B♭4–D5–F5 ascending, lowest = tonic B♭. With explicit caveat that in the genuine Op.4 D-major autograph the transposed equivalent is A–F♯–D with lowest = tonic D.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The factual core is now stable across rounds.

Symphony No.2 B.12 was signed Op.4 by Dvořák in 1865/70 in D major. The 1888 revision/transposition down a major third was published as Op.22 in B♭ major and is the version in virtually all modern scores, habitually cited in the literature as “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12”.

* Original Op.4 / autograph D major: Finale IV Allegro vivace closes tutti in D. First violins end with the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D, conventionally read in score order as the descent A–F♯–D held on the final D-major fermata. Distinct pitch-classes attacked: A, F♯, D. In the descending reading the last attack is the tonic D and that D is the lowest of the three successive first-violin attacks. In the upward engraving the lowest written attack is F♯. Pitch-class mapping B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A.

* Op.22 / performing B♭ major edition: same music transposed. First-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio, score order descending F5–D5–B♭4, equivalently ascending B♭4–D5–F5. Distinct pitches: B♭, D, F. Last attack in descending reading is tonic B♭, which is also the lowest of the three successive attacks, conventionally written B♭4 in the modern edition ≈ B♭3 in older engraving.

Round 4 public positions have fully converged on this dual description. Colleagues 1,2,6,8 foreground the performing/revised identification: the edition catalogued/performed today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major version and the lowest first-violin note of the three-note close is tonic B♭, last of F–D–B♭. Colleagues 3,4,5,7 foreground the strict catalogue reading: Op.4 B.12 is the 1865 D-major autograph, Op.22 is the later transposition; for the original Op.4 the lowest/last first-violin note is tonic D of A–F♯–D. All eight now state both readings explicitly and give the transposition mapping B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A.

Earlier errors about order/octave – e.g. F5–B♭5–D6, G''–A''–B♭'' turn, b♭''–g'–e♭' dominant-seventh, and the “F♯ is lowest” misreading of the upward engraving – have been corrected. Current consensus is D is lowest in descending original reading, B♭ is lowest in descending performing reading.

Persisting disagreement is interpretive, not factual: whether the question intends the strict original Op.4 key D major, i.e. lowest = D, or the familiar B♭-major performing transposition that is commonly labelled Symphony No.2 Op.4, i.e. lowest = B♭. Exact octave designation across autograph/Breitkopf/modern editions remains unresolved, but pitch-class identity is settled.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The edition identity issue is now essentially settled in the group as a duality rather than a pure dispute.

Performing / revised reading that all colleagues now reference as the edition actually in use today under the heading “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12”:
* The work habitually cited and performed as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the 1888 Breitkopf & Härtel revision / Op.22 transposition of B.12 down a major third to B♭ major.
* IV Allegro vivace / Allegro con brio closes tutti in B♭ major. First-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic broken chord.
* In score order the three successive attacks are written Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, i.e. the same pitch-class set as the ascending arpeggio B♭4 – D5 – F5.
* The three distinct pitch classes sounded are B♭, D, F. The last attack held with the fermata is the tonic B♭, the bottom of the descending F–D–B♭ arpeggio.
* Lowest of the three successive attacks in the performing edition is the tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 in modern printing, ~B♭3 in older engraving.

Original Op.4 D-major reading that is now acknowledged by all:
* B.12 as signed by Dvořák in 1865/70 is Symphony No.2 Op.4 in D major. Op.22 is the later revision/transposition to B♭ major.
* IV closes tutti in D major on D-major tonic triad. First-violin coda is engraved up F♯–A–D and read in score order as the descent A – F♯ – D.
* Three distinct pitch classes attacked are A, F♯, D. In descending reading the last attack held with fermata is tonic D, the lowest of the three successive attacks.
* Transposition mapping: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. The familiar F–D–B♭ close is the transposition of the original A–F♯–D / F♯–A–D close. The performing B♭ is the transposed equivalent of the original tonic D.

Observed corrections and shifts:
* Colleague 2 now explicitly acknowledges the original D-major autograph while maintaining the performing B♭ identification.
* Colleague 3 now states the catalogue Op.4 B.12 is D major and Op.22 is the B♭ performing transposition.
* Colleague 7 drops the earlier G–A–B♭ turn / E♭ dominant-seventh figuration and aligns with the F–D–B♭ arpeggio with the original D-major note.
* Colleague 4 earlier F5–B♭5–D6 wording is now superseded by the consensus F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭4–D5–F5 description.
Octave naming remains loose but pitch-class identity is consistent.

Unresolved intentional ambiguity: The question literally asks for Symphony no.2 Op.4. Strict catalogue designation points to the 1865/70 D-major autograph, whose lowest first-violin note of the three-note close is tonic D. The edition that dominates modern scores and common reference, and which all colleagues identify as the work now habitually labelled Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12, is the B♭-major performing version, whose lowest first-violin note of the three-note close is tonic B♭. The group remains bifurcated on which intended reading the question demands.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Op.4/B.12 identity split is now explicit and acknowledged across the group.

Performing/revised B♭-major reading, majority public position:
* Colleagues 1,2,6,8 state the edition that is catalogued and performed today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the 1888 revised/Op.22 transposition down a major third to B♭ major.
* IV closes tutti in B♭ major. First-violin coda is tonic arpeggio in score order Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, same pitch-class set as ascending B♭4 – D5 – F5.
* Three attacks are B♭, D, F. Last attack held with fermata is tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 in modern edition ≈ B♭3 in older engraving, the lowest of the three successive attacks in the descending reading.
* Musicological note now repeated by all B♭ advocates: autograph Op.4 B.12 1865/70 was in D major, transposed B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A in 1888 revision published as Op.22.

Original-autograph D-major reading, minority/catalogue-correct position:
* Colleagues 3,4,5,7 hold B.12 as signed 1865/70 is the D-major symphony; Op.22 is the 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major.
* In genuine Op.4 autograph IV Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major. First-violin coda is D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order as descent A – F♯ – D.
* Three pitch classes attacked are F♯, A, D. In descending reading the last and lowest successive attack is tonic D, the note held with final fermata; in upward written order F♯–A–D the lowest written attack is F♯ ≈ F♯4.
* Persistent claim: Op.4 reading is D as final/lowest successive attack, F♯ as lowest written attack.

Transposition mapping is now consistently given by all: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. Hence performing F5–D5–B♭4 = original A–F♯–D. B♭ is lowest only in the transposed performing version; D is lowest in original key.

Unresolved intent remains the core disagreement: whether the question intends the standard published/performing B♭-major version, in which the lowest first-violin pitch of the closing three-note figure is B♭, or the original-autograph D-major Op.4 reading, in which the three pitch classes are F♯, A, D and the last/lowest successive attack is tonic D with F♯ the lowest written attack in the upward engraving. Octave placement varies by edition but pitch-class content is either B♭–D–F in the B♭ performing edition or F♯–A–D in the D-major original. The B♭ answers remain the majority public position, while the D-major/original-transposition argument is now more explicitly articulated and acknowledged even by B♭-major colleagues.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is fundamentally ambiguous between catalogue Op.4 B.12 and the edition that is habitually performed/cited today as “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12”.

Catalogue-correct reading:
* B.12 as signed by Dvořák 1865/70 is Symphony No.2 Op.4 in D major. Op.22 is the 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major.
* In the genuine Op.4 / autograph IV Allegro vivace closes tutti in D major on the D-major tonic triad. Engraved up Vln I F♯–A–D, read in score order as the descent A – F♯ – D. Three pitch classes attacked: A, F♯, D. In the descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack is the tonic D and it is the bottom of the three-note termination. Conventionally written about D5 in the first-violin staff, the last/lowest first-violin note is the tonic D.

Performing-edition / mislabelled reading:
* The 1888 revision published as Op.22 was transposed B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A and is the version in everyday use, habitually catalogued as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 in B♭ major.
* In that performing edition the first-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic broken chord Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4 in score order, i.e. B♭4 – D5 – F5 ascending. Pitch-class set B♭, D, F. In the descending reading F > D > B♭ the last attack held with the final fermata is the tonic B♭ and it is the bottom of the arpeggio, conventionally written B♭4 ~ B♭3 in older engraving.

Round 4 status:
Colleagues 1,2,6,8 present the performing-edition answer first – lowest/last first-violin pitch is the tonic B♭, B♭4, with an explicit musicological note that this is the transposed equivalent of the original Op.4 tonic D.
Colleagues 3,4,5,7 present the catalogue-correct answer first – lowest/last first-violin pitch in the genuine Op.4 autograph is the tonic D, ~D5, the transposed equivalent of the performing B♭.
All eight now agree on the transposition mapping and that the source of disagreement is conflation of Op.4 with its Op.22 transposition. Earlier odd readings G–A–B♭ etc. are superseded; the consistent description is F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F ↔ A–F♯–D / F♯–A–D.

Unresolved nuance remains which interpretation the questioner intends: strictly catalogue Op.4 B.12 → lowest is D; the edition most people mean when they say “Symphony No.2 Op.4” today → lowest is B♭. The persistent practical answer heard in performance is B♭4, the musicological correct Op.4 answer is D.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The work is B.12, signed Symphony No.2 Op.4 in 1865/70 in D major; the 1888 revision is a major-third transposition down to B♭ major, published as Op.22, but the B♭ performing / Breitkopf & Härtel version is the one in everyday use and is universally labelled today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Performing / everyday B♭ edition:
IV. Allegro vivace / Allegro con brio closes tutti in B♭ major. First-violin coda is the B♭-major tonic broken chord written in score order Vln I F5 – D5 – B♭4, the same pitch-class set as the ascending reading B♭4 – D5 – F5. Three distinct attacks are B♭, D, F. In the descending reading the last attack held with the fermata is also the bottom of the arpeggio: tonic B♭, conventionally B♭4 in modern printing ~ B♭3/4 in older engraving. This is the lowest first-violin pitch in the edition habitually cited as Op.4 B.12. Colleagues 1,2,6,8 in round 4 explicitly defend this as the practical answer.

Strict catalogue / autograph Op.4 B.12:
B.12 as signed by Dvořák is the D-major autograph. In the original key the same figure is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and read in part as the descent A – F♯ – D. Three distinct pitch classes attacked are A, F♯, D. In the normal descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack and bottom of the arpeggio is tonic D, conventionally about D5 in the first-violin staff, the transposed equivalent of the performing B♭. Colleagues 3,4,5,7 in round 4 insist the Op.4 label strictly denotes the D-major autograph, so the catalogue-correct lowest first-violin note is tonic D, with B♭ being the Op.22 transposed equivalent.

Transposition relation is stable and agreed across rounds: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A. F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F is the transposition of F♯–A–D / A–F♯–D.

Unresolved technical points persist: exact octave nomenclature B♭4 vs B♭3/4, D5 vs older engraving, and whether “three notes” is meant as the three successive attacks F–D–B♭ before the sustained final chord or the sustained triad itself. Pitch-class answer is stable under the performing edition = tonic B♭; under strict original Op.4 identification = tonic D. The deliberation remains split between the practical/performing identification of Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 = B♭ major, lowest = B♭, and the musicologically strict identification Op.4 B.12 = D major autograph, lowest = D.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The musicological facts are now stable across rounds. B.12 Symphony No.2 Op.4 1865/70 autograph is D major; the 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major was published as Op.22 and is the version in everyday use, habitually cited in libraries and performance material as “Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12”.

Finale IV Allegro vivace / Allegro con brio coda first-violin termination:
* Original Op.4 B.12 D major: engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order as descent A–F♯–D, held on final D-major fermata. Three pitch classes A, F♯, D. Last attack is tonic D and that D is the bottom of the three successive attacks, conventionally D5 in violin staff.
* Performing / Op.22 transposition B♭ major: same figure is B♭–D–F. Modern editions write in score order F5–D5–B♭4, i.e. ascending B♭4–D5–F5. Three pitch classes B♭, D, F. Last attack is tonic B♭ and that B♭ is the bottom of the three successive attacks, conventionally B♭4.

Transposition mapping is consistently B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A, so performing lowest B♭ is transposed equivalent of original D.

Round 4 public positions:
Colleagues 1,2,6,8 now state the edition catalogued/performed today under the heading Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the 1888 B♭-major Op.22 performing version, with first-violin close F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭4–D5–F5 and lowest note tonic B♭, with a musicological note about the D-major autograph.
Colleagues 3,4,5,7 hold literal catalogue designation: Op.4 B.12 = D-major autograph, lowest/final first-violin note of the three-note close is tonic D, and note that the familiar B♭ answer is the Op.22 performing transposition.

Earlier erroneous subsidiary claims about register/order have been corrected in round 3. Unresolved nuance remains which reading the question intends: literal catalogue Op.4 B.12 → lowest D; modern performing usage mislabelled Op.4 → lowest B♭. My best belief for the literal Op.4 as signed is D-major tonic D as last and lowest of A–F♯–D; the B♭ answer is the transposed Op.22 performing version that dominates current practice.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation is now focused on the IV. Allegro vivace/Allegro con brio coda of B.12 and the Op.4/Op.22 identification problem.

Performing/revised material that is in everyday use and universally labelled today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12:
* The work is the 1888 Breitkopf & Härtel performing/revised version, published as Op.22, a transposition down a major third from the autograph to B♭ major.
* First-violin coda in score order is the B♭-major tonic broken chord written descending F5 – D5 – B♭4, the same pitch set read ascending B♭4 – D5 – F5.
* Three distinct attacks are B♭, D, F. The last attack held with the final tutti fermata is the tonic B♭, the bottom of the F–D–B♭ descent. In modern edition that is B♭4, ~B♭3 in older engraving. This is the lowest of the three-note closing gesture in the edition actually performed and catalogued as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Original-key/autograph material:
* B.12 as signed Op.4 in 1865/70 is the D-major symphony. Op.22 is the later 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major.
* In the genuine Op.4 autograph/original IV closes tutti in D major. First-violin coda is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and conventionally read in score order as the descent A – F♯ – D.
* Three distinct pitch classes are A, F♯, D. The last attack and the lowest of the three successive attacks is the tonic D, normally printed about D5 in the violin part.
* Transposition B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A maps the familiar performing F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F onto the original A–F♯–D / F♯–A–D. The performing tonic B♭ is the transposed equivalent of the autograph tonic D.

Positions and shifts in round 4:
* Colleagues 1,2,6,8 state explicitly the edition in practical use labelled Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major performing/revised version, lowest first-violin note is tonic B♭, with a musicological note about the D-major autograph.
* Colleagues 3,4,5,7 state both facts: the Op.4 catalogue designation is the D-major autograph with lowest D, and the Op.22/B♭ performing transposition now habitually cited as Op.4 has lowest B♭. Colleague 5 emphasizes the “lowest = B♭” answer is the Op.22 performing transposition, not the Op.4 autograph that the opus number denotes.
* Earlier outlier readings G–A–B♭ turn and B♭–g′–e♭′ dominant-seventh termination are not repeated. Earlier confusion in Colleague 4 about F5–B♭5–D6 and “lowest = D” in degree terms is now reconciled to F5–D5–B♭4 with B♭ as bottom.
* Colleague 2 has moved to the B♭-major performing reading with an explicit musicological note that the autograph Op.4 was originally D major and later transposed to B♭ for Op.22, now rejecting earlier D-major-only readings.
* Colleague 7 no longer treats the D-major reading as mistaken; it now presents both the catalogue Op.4 D-major original and the performing Op.22 B♭ transposition.

Current understanding:
In the edition most players use and which is universally identified today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12, the first-violin three-note close is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest note is the tonic B♭, written B♭4 in the modern edition, last attack of the descent.
If the question is taken literally for the original Op.4 autograph key, the pitch-class equivalent is D major and the lowest of the three successive first-violin attacks is the tonic D, which transposes to B♭ in the familiar B♭-major performing version.
The musicological fact of the transposition is now essentially agreed; the unresolved interpretive issue remains whether the question intends the performing Op.22 material habitually cited as Op.4 B.12 or the autograph Op.4 D-major original that the opus number denotes.

reflection_text.2:
The work is B.12, signed Symphony No.2 Op.4 in 1865/70. Autograph/genuine Op.4 is D major; the 1888 revision/transposition down a major third to B♭ major was published as Op.22 and is the version in everyday use and habitually cited today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Coda of IV Allegro vivace/Allegro molto:
* Original Op.4 D-major autograph: first-violin coda is the D-major tonic broken chord, engraved up F♯–A–D, read in score order A–F♯–D. Three distinct pitch classes A, F♯, D. In descending reading the last attack/lowest of the three successive notes is tonic D. This is maintained by Colleagues 3,4,5,7.
* Performing/revised B♭-major edition, the edition universally quoted today as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12: first-violin Vln I in score order F5–D5–B♭4, i.e. pitch-class set B♭4–D5–F5 ascending. Three distinct attacks are B♭–D–F. Last attack is tonic B♭, also bottom of descending arpeggio. This is stated as primary by Colleagues 1,2,6,8 and acknowledged as the transposed equivalent by all.

Transposition map is now explicitly acknowledged by all: B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A; so B♭-major F–D–B♭ = D-major A–F♯–D.

Round 0 errors corrected in prior rounds: Colleague 4’s F5–B♭5–D6 / “lowest degree D” retracted to F5–D5–B♭4 / tonic B♭ lowest; Colleague 7’s G–A–B♭ turn retracted.

Round 4 consensus: Colleagues 1,2,6,8 give the performing edition answer as primary: lowest first-violin note is tonic B♭, written B♭4 ~ B♭3 in older engraving, last of F5–D5–B♭4 descending ≡ B♭4–D5–F5 ascending. Colleagues 3,4,5,7 give the catalogue-original answer as primary: lowest first-violin note in the genuine Op.4 B.12 autograph is tonic D, last of A–F♯–D descending ≡ F♯–A–D engraved up, and note that B♭ is the transposed equivalent in Op.22.

Unresolved is intent of the question: original Op.4 D-major autograph → pitch-class answer D, lowest first-violin note tonic D; or standard modern performing edition commonly called Symphony No.2 Op.4 → pitch-class answer B♭, lowest first-violin note tonic B♭.

My current best belief remains the conventional modern performing reading quoted in the deliberation: Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 as performed today is in B♭ major, first-violin final three pitches F5–D5–B♭4 descending ≡ B♭4–D5–F5 ascending, lowest = tonic B♭. With explicit caveat that in the genuine Op.4 D-major autograph the transposed equivalent is A–F♯–D with lowest = tonic D.

Performing / everyday B♭ edition:
IV. Allegro vivace / Allegro con brio closes tutti in B♭ major. Strict catalogue / autograph Op.4 B.12:
B.12 as signed by Dvořák is the D-major autograph. In the original key the same figure is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and read in part as the descent A – F♯ – D. Three distinct pitch classes attacked are A, F♯, D. In the normal descending reading A > F♯ > D the last attack and bottom of the arpeggio is tonic D, conventionally about D5 in the first-violin staff, the transposed equivalent of the performing B♭. Colleagues 3,4,5,7 in round 4 insist the Op.4 label strictly denotes the D-major autograph, so the catalogue-correct lowest first-violin note is tonic D, with B♭ being the Op.22 transposed equivalent.

reflection_text.1:
The deliberation is now focused on the IV. Allegro vivace/Allegro con brio coda of B.12 and the Op.4/Op.22 identification problem.

Performing/revised material that is in everyday use and universally labelled today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12:
* The work is the 1888 Breitkopf & Härtel performing/revised version, published as Op.22, a transposition down a major third from the autograph to B♭ major.
* First-violin coda in score order is the B♭-major tonic broken chord written descending F5 – D5 – B♭4, the same pitch set read ascending B♭4 – D5 – F5.
* Three distinct attacks are B♭, D, F. The last attack held with the final tutti fermata is the tonic B♭, the bottom of the F–D–B♭ descent. In modern edition that is B♭4, ~B♭3 in older engraving. This is the lowest of the three-note closing gesture in the edition actually performed and catalogued as Sym. No.2 Op.4 B.12.

Original-key/autograph material:
* B.12 as signed Op.4 in 1865/70 is the D-major symphony. Op.22 is the later 1888 revision transposed down a major third to B♭ major.
* In the genuine Op.4 autograph/original IV closes tutti in D major. First-violin coda is the D-major tonic broken chord engraved up F♯–A–D and conventionally read in score order as the descent A – F♯ – D.
* Three distinct pitch classes are A, F♯, D. The last attack and the lowest of the three successive attacks is the tonic D, normally printed about D5 in the violin part.
* Transposition B♭→D, D→F♯, F→A maps the familiar performing F5–D5–B♭4 / B♭–D–F onto the original A–F♯–D / F♯–A–D. The performing tonic B♭ is the transposed equivalent of the autograph tonic D.

Positions and shifts in round 4:
* Colleagues 1,2,6,8 state explicitly the edition in practical use labelled Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12 is the B♭-major performing/revised version, lowest first-violin note is tonic B♭, with a musicological note about the D-major autograph.
* Colleagues 3,4,5,7 state both facts: the Op.4 catalogue designation is the D-major autograph with lowest D, and the Op.22/B♭ performing transposition now habitually cited as Op.4 has lowest B♭. Colleague 5 emphasizes the “lowest = B♭” answer is the Op.22 performing transposition, not the Op.4 autograph that the opus number denotes.
* Earlier outlier readings G–A–B♭ turn and B♭–g′–e♭′ dominant-seventh termination are not repeated. Earlier confusion in Colleague 4 about F5–B♭5–D6 and “lowest = D” in degree terms is now reconciled to F5–D5–B♭4 with B♭ as bottom.
* Colleague 2 has moved to the B♭-major performing reading with an explicit musicological note that the autograph Op.4 was originally D major and later transposed to B♭ for Op.22, now rejecting earlier D-major-only readings.
* Colleague 7 no longer treats the D-major reading as mistaken; it now presents both the catalogue Op.4 D-major original and the performing Op.22 B♭ transposition.

Current understanding:
In the edition most players use and which is universally identified today as Symphony No.2 Op.4 B.12, the first-violin three-note close is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ and the lowest note is the tonic B♭, written B♭4 in the modern edition, last attack of the descent.
If the question is taken literally for the original Op.4 autograph key, the pitch-class equivalent is D major and the lowest of the three successive first-violin attacks is the tonic D, which transposes to B♭ in the familiar B♭-major performing version.
The musicological fact of the transposition is now essentially agreed; the unresolved interpretive issue remains whether the question intends the performing Op.22 material habitually cited as Op.4 B.12 or the autograph Op.4 D-major original that the opus number denotes.
